# An invariant positive buffer breaks the two-parity deepest tie

This is an exact actual-body calibration of the energy-power buffer. The
unbuffered family, all-normal depth certificate, and strict nonheavy/minor
quotas are proved in
`candidate 75dd33535e246a34`.
Here its POSITIVE-buffer maximum is computed, rather than inferred from
its two ordinary deepest sources. No bad-depth or OC counterexample is
asserted.

## 1. Body, ordinary depth, and invariant normalization

The four interval fibers at integer bases 0,1,2,3 are

    K0=[47/50,26/25],  K1=[-11/10,1],
    K2=[-23/25,23/25], K3=[-9/100,9/100].

Their convex lower and concave upper endpoint interpolations define a
full-dimensional convex body. Their lengths are

    l0=1/10, l1=21/10, l2=46/25, l3=9/50,
    M=211/50.

The original global raw depth is Q=11/10, attained exactly at (1,0) and
(2,0), with all slopes and closed pure-base halfspaces certified in the
cited source. Every fiber is strictly lighter than M/2; all strict proper
closed-minor occupied-parity count quotas hold.

The within-fiber covariance in continuous dimension one is

    Sigma=(sum_i li^3)/(12M)=1937167/6330000,
    c^2=Sigma/M=1937167/26712600.                         (1)

For an interval [l,u] of length L and midpoint m, its projective energy
at y in that interval is

    E(y)=4(y-l)(u-y)/L=L-4(y-m)^2/L.                      (2)

It vanishes at the endpoints. Use the invariant buffer with
f_i(y)=sqrt(E_i(y)/M) and covector norm Gamma(u)=sqrt(Sigma)|u|.
After dividing a nonzero continuous normal by its absolute value, the
buffered threshold displacement is

    delta_i(y)=epsilon c sqrt(E_i(y)).                   (3)

Thus all nonvertical buffered caps at (p,y) are

    x>=y+t(z-p)-delta_p(y),
    x<=y+t(z-p)+delta_p(y),                             (4)

for arbitrary real t. Pure-base CLOSED cap masses are unchanged.
The same actual body and its original measure are used throughout.

## 2. Exact values at the two original deepest marks

Set E1=E_1(0), E2=E_2(0). Directly from (2),

    E1=44/21, E2=46/25, E1-E2=134/525>0.                 (5)

Write delta_i=epsilon c sqrt(Ei). We shall prove, for

    0<epsilon<=1/10000,                                (6)

that

    b_epsilon(1,0)=Q+delta_1,
    b_epsilon(2,0)=Q+delta_2.                           (7)

For the lower bounds, every original nonvertical cap through either mark
has mass at least Q. Its own interval threshold is at zero. Enlarging
that cap by delta_i increases its OWN captured length exactly delta_i,
while each other contribution is nondecreasing. All own endpoints are
farther than delta_i from zero. Thus every cap in (4) has mass at least
Q+delta_i. The smallest pure-base masses are 11/5 at base1 and 101/50 at
base2, both strictly larger than Q+delta_i.

For matching upper bounds, use the following original critical caps:

    H+ : x-(z-1)>=0,
    H- : -x-(93/100)(z-1)>=0,
    J+ : x+2(z-2)>=0,
    J- : -x+2(z-2)>=0.                                 (8)

At base1, H+ has K0 strictly full, own K1 proper, and K2,K3 strictly
empty. H- has only its own K1 proper and every other fiber strictly
empty. The smallest external status margin of these two caps is 1/100.
At base2, each J cap has K3 strictly full, own K2 proper, and K0,K1
strictly empty. Their external margins exceed 1/100. Replacing the right
side in (8) by -delta_i preserves these statuses and adds exactly delta_i
to the own captured length. This proves (7).

## 3. No other continuous mark or integer base wins

Here are explicit bounds that retain the whole continuum of candidate
marks. Let eta=1/1000. Since E_i(y)<=li<=21/10, put

    delta_max=epsilon c sqrt(21/10).

The exact number

    c^2(21/10)=13560169/89042000<1

shows delta_max<epsilon<=1/10000. Each of four interval contributions
can increase by at most delta_max upon buffer enlargement; hence, at
EVERY original actual point w,

    b_epsilon(w)<=b_0(w)+4delta_max.                    (9)

This remains valid if a pure-base cap is the ordinary infimum, because
such a cap is unchanged. It also follows by taking an approximating
sequence of nonvertical cap slopes; no attaining-slope assumption is
needed for (9).

For |y|<=eta in either inner fiber, the appropriate caps (8) still have
their original external statuses after shifting the source to y and
adding its buffer: |y|+delta_i(y)<11/10000<1/100. They therefore give

    b_epsilon(i,y)<=Q-|y|+epsilon c sqrt(E_i(y)), i=1,2. (10)

On these neighborhoods E_i(y)>1 and |E_i'(y)|<1 by the explicit formula
(2). Also c<1. Consequently the last term in (10) has absolute derivative
less than epsilon/2<1. The right side is uniquely maximized at y=0.
In combination with (7), this proves that the unique maximizing point
within each neighborhood is the original marked point, with values (7).
This argument includes the first interval's noncentral ordinary mark:
its midpoint is -1/20, not zero.

For points of inner fibers with |y|>=eta, tighten H+ or H-, respectively
J+ or J-, by the fixed amount eta toward the sign of y. The resulting
closed cap still contains that point, preserves all external statuses,
and has original mass Q-eta. Thus their old depths are at most Q-eta.
At either extreme base the own interval can be isolated by a sufficiently
steep tilt; the old depth is at most half its length, hence at most9/100.
Formula (9) now gives, everywhere outside the two neighborhoods,

    b_epsilon<=max(Q-eta,9/100)+4delta_max
             <Q-3/5000<Q.                             (11)

Equations (5), (7), (10), and (11) prove the complete conclusion:

    max_S b_epsilon=11/10+epsilon sqrt(Sigma/M) sqrt(44/21),
    the unique maximizing point is (1,0),
    I_epsilon={1},
    for EVERY epsilon in (0,1/10000].                  (12)

In particular the maximizing base set changes from the two original
parities at epsilon=0 to one parity for every positive epsilon in this
range. The normalized buffered maximum is (12) divided by the unchanged
original M.

## 4. The actual nonzero buffered normal resultant

The displaced versions of H+ and H- in (8) form a fully regular attaining
two-row group at the unique buffered source. Normalize their continuous
normals to u+=1/sqrt(Sigma), u-=-1/sqrt(Sigma); their integer coefficients
are a+=-1/sqrt(Sigma), a-=-(93/100)/sqrt(Sigma).

From (2), E_1'(0)=-4/21. Consequently

    delta_1'(0)=-delta_1/22.

The exact positive normalized source-balance coefficients are

    rho+=(1-delta_1/22)/2,
    rho-=(1+delta_1/22)/2.                             (13)

Indeed rho+u++rho-u-=epsilon f_1'(0). Both rows have only the proper own
section, so their mixed coareas in this normalization are both
sqrt(Sigma). Their actual response weights therefore also equal rho+,
rho-. The ordinary projective optimizer at the marked point is a_opt=-1/22,
so this is precisely the advertised nonzero relation

    sum rho u=epsilon f_1(0) a_opt.

No ordinary zero-resultant circuit has been substituted for this group.
Its source's minimal deepest-base face is the singleton {1}. The loss of
one occupied deepest parity is caused by the actual, strictly different
energy values (5), not by a rounding convention or by dropping boundary
mass. This example does not prove that buffering always reduces a
saturated parity cover.
